name: Lalbagh Botanical Garden
label: Lalbagh
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Glass House' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'BBMP Glass House' (way/317489528): middle (76 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W15802464 (Lalbagh Botanical Gardens): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic botanical garden with a glass house.

text.description:
Lalbagh is a large botanical garden in Bangalore, and its Glass House is the structure most visitors want a picture of. Guides call it the garden's most photographed building, and it is easy to see why. The iron-and-glass facade and the dome sit behind an open lawn, so the whole building fits in one frame without you having to step back into the trees.

The best photo is the classic head-on view. From the south lawn, facing the facade, you can line up the dome in the middle of the frame and let the building look symmetrical. One guide recommends doing this in the morning, and that suits a phone well, because the glass is less likely to blow out to white in softer light. The inside of the Glass House is normally closed, so plan to shoot the outside unless a flower show is on.

If you have time, the garden has other good frames. Lalbagh Rock is a granite outcrop with a wide view over the treetops and the city, and a 16th-century watchtower stands there. The lake bridge gives tree reflections on still water, with a small island and tree-lined banks on both sides. Both make a nice second or third picture after the Glass House.

Take your time on the lawn. Walk a few steps left or right until the dome is centred, and keep an eye out for people crossing the grass, who can add scale or spoil the symmetry.
text.geographic_location: Lalbagh Botanical Garden is a large public garden in Bangalore. The Glass House stands on a lawn inside the garden.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so make your own way to Lalbagh Botanical Garden in Bangalore. Once inside the garden, head for the Glass House and its south lawn, which is where the classic head-on view is taken. Check the garden's official site for which gate to use. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the lawn, which lets the whole facade and dome fit with a little grass in front. If the lawn is busy and you have to stand close, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to keep the dome in frame, and keep the phone level so the sides do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Glass House (front lawn to the south, facing the facade). The full iron-and-glass facade and dome of the Glass House, framed across the open lawn. Inside the garden, stand on the south lawn in front of the Glass House, facing the facade. From here the full iron-and-glass front and the dome are framed across the open grass.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the dome on the centre line, so the two halves of the building mirror each other. Keep some lawn in the bottom of the frame to lead the eye in. For a different view, Lalbagh Rock gives a wide shot over the treetops and city with the old watchtower, and the lake bridge gives tree reflections on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glass or the dome to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright glass keeps its detail and does not turn white.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before about 10 AM, when the light is best and the glass is less likely to be overexposed.

text.access_note: Lalbagh is a garden with a gate, so check the official site before you go, and check on the day whether phone photography is free.

name: Bangalore Palace
label: Bangalore Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palace Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Palace Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/143384387: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bangalore Palace' (126 m across).

text.description:
Bangalore Palace is a royal palace built for Chamarajendra Wadiyar X, the Maharaja of Mysore, and commissioned in 1873. Its design is based on Windsor Castle in England, in the Tudor Revival style, so it looks more like a small English castle than anything else in the city. That makes it easy to photograph. You get large fortified towers, turreted parapets and walls partly covered in climbing plants, all set behind open lawns. The palace has about 34 rooms and sits roughly 5.3 km north of the city centre.

For a first picture, start on Palace Road in front of the ornate main gate. From here you can photograph the gateway and the approach to the grounds, with the first glimpse of the palace facade beyond. The gate details are worth a close-up. Once you are inside the grounds, the full front view with the turrets framed against lawn and sky is the classic shot. If it is busy, the rear and side of the palace with the garden in the foreground is a quieter alternative.

The grounds are used for concerts, fairs and weddings, so the scene can change from day to day. Interior photography is restricted, so ask at the entrance before taking your phone inside. Some rooms may also be closed for renovation.
text.geographic_location: Bangalore Palace is in the north of Bangalore, about 5.3 km north of the city centre.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop information is available for this spot. The palace is about 5.3 km north of the city centre. The palace itself lies to the north-east of that point, about 7 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and the first glimpse of the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole gateway and lawns in one frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the turrets and gate details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Palace Road (in front of the palace's ornate main gate). The ornate gateway and the approach to the palace grounds, with the first glimpse of the facade beyond. From here you see the ornate gateway and the approach to the palace grounds, with the first glimpse of the facade beyond. The palace itself is to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the gate in the foreground, with the palace sitting beyond it. Move closer to photograph the gate's detailing. For the full front view of the turrets against lawn and sky, or the quieter rear and side view with the garden in front, you will need to go into the grounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate or the palace walls to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail. Keep the phone level to stop the towers leaning.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when the low light is soft and warm on the gate and facade.

text.access_note: The palace complex is open to visitors, but entry and photography rules (especially indoors) can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Golden hour is a good time to photograph the main gate and facade.
Interior photography is restricted, so ask at the entrance before photographing inside.
The rear and side view of the palace is usually less crowded than the front view.
Some rooms may be closed for renovation.

name: M. Chinnaswamy Stadium
label: Chinnaswamy Stadium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'G Upper stand, M. Chinnaswamy Stadium' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1861907: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: M. Chinnaswamy Stadium is Bengaluru's best-known cricket ground, on the edge of Cubbon Park and close to MG Road. Work began in 1970, and the first Test was played here in November 1974. It holds about 40,000 people and is home to Karnataka's teams and to Royal Challengers Bangalore, whose red and yellow colours give the place a bold look. It was also the first cricket stadium in the world to use solar panels for much of its electricity. For a phone photographer the appeal is the sheer shape of the place: a big open bowl, a neat green field and the pitch at its centre. The best view recommended here is from the upper tier of the G stand, which looks across the whole ground. That makes it a good spot for wide, sweeping shots rather than close-ups. Seats in the stands need a ticket, so this is not a free roadside viewpoint. If you only want the outside, the front facade with its large lettering can be framed from Queens Road at gates 1 and 2. Crowds build up outside on big match days, so take the outside shot on a quieter day. Photography rules inside have varied over the years, and the stadium has had restrictions on large events since 2025. Check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of Bangalore, beside Cubbon Park and Queens Road, a short distance from MG Road.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Queens Road at the edge of Cubbon Park, near MG Road, by taxi or hired scooter. The stadium is next to Cubbon Park and Queens Road. On match days expect heavy crowds around the gates, so allow extra time and follow the signs for your stand. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole bowl, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the field. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the pitch, the scoreboard or players.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The best-view recommendation is the upper tier of the G stand, which gives a wide view of the whole field and pitch and suits panoramic shots of the ground. This needs a ticket for an event. If you are only outside, the front facade is shown from Queens Road at gates 1 and 2, with the big 'Chinnaswamy Stadium' lettering.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the field filling the lower half and the opposite stands and sky above. Try panorama mode for the full curve of the bowl, moving slowly and steadily. For a second viewpoint, the N stand also gives a view of the whole ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the field to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the stands. If the crowd is moving, take a Live Photo or a burst and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a ticketed match or event day for the full atmosphere. If it is an evening event under floodlights, try night mode and hold the phone steady against the rail or your arm. For the outside facade, pick a quieter non-event day.

text.access_note: The best viewpoint is inside the stadium and needs a ticket for an event, so check the official site before you go for current rules and which stands are open.

name: Cubbon Park
label: Cubbon Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'State Central Library' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'State Central Library' (way/52032473): middle (61 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/22895320: large area 'Cubbon Park' (1823 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large green park in the city centre.

text.description:
Cubbon Park is the big green lung of central Bangalore, laid out in 1870 and named after Sir Mark Cubbon, a long-serving commissioner. It began at around 100 acres and is now reported to cover about 300. It has been renamed more than once: in 1927 it became Sri Chamarajendra Park, and it is formerly known as Cubbon Park. The landscaping mixes rock outcrops, bamboo, tree-lined avenues, lawns and flowerbeds, with colonial-era buildings dotted through it.

For a phone photo, the best place to start is the State Central Library, which sits in Iyer Hall with a rose garden at its front. The red-brick building behind rose beds and winding walking paths makes a neat, classic park picture, and it shows the park's mix of greenery and old architecture in one frame. Look for the library and rose garden nearby, then find your frame.

If you have time, two other landmarks at the park's edge make good alternatives. Attara Kacheri, built in 1864 and now the High Court, is a red stone building that looks striking against green trees. Vidhana Soudha, the large domed building across the road, is a shot of the building itself rather than of the park. Wander the paths between shots: the avenues are shady and quiet, and early morning is when walkers and joggers use them.
text.geographic_location: Cubbon Park is in the heart of Bangalore's Central Business District, a short distance from M.G. Road, Kasturba Road and Hudson Circle. Attara Kacheri (the High Court) and Vidhana Soudha stand at its edge.
text.directions_text: Head for the park and the State Central Library. The park can be entered from M.G. Road, Kasturba Road, Hudson Circle or Ambedkar Veedhi. A metro station called Cubbon Park is reported to be very close to one of the park's entrances. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the library with the rose beds in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to fit the whole building and the paths in, and to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for brickwork and roses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at State Central Library (front lawn and rose beds beside the building, inside the park). The red-brick library building framed by rose beds and the park's walking paths, a classic colonial-style park shot. The library's front lawn is the viewpoint inside the park, looking at the red-brick building across the rose beds. From the viewpoint the walking paths and rose beds lead the eye towards the library.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the rose beds or a curving path in the foreground, with the library behind. Turn on gridlines and keep the building's vertical lines straight. Crouch a little for the flowers to fill the lower part of the frame. For something different, walk to the edge of the park for Attara Kacheri (red stone against green trees) or Vidhana Soudha (a shot of the building, not the park).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the red brick to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky is not washed out and the brick colour stays rich. Use portrait mode for close shots of the roses.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the lawns. Early morning is also when the park is full of walkers.

text.access_note: Cubbon Park is a public park, but opening days, hours and photography rules can vary (large cameras and tripods may need permission), so check the official site on the day before you go; phone photos should be fine.

name: UB City
label: UB City
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vittal Mallya Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Vittal Mallya Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/38773290: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'UB City' (327 m across).

text.description:
UB City is a cluster of six buildings in central Bengaluru, built on about 13 acres by the UB Group together with Prestige Group. It mixes offices, luxury shops and service apartments, and it has four towers. One of them, UB Tower, carries a rooftop helipad. The complex stands opposite Cubbon Park, so its glass and steel lines sit right beside one of the city's green spaces.

It photographs well because the building is big, clean and strongly geometric. The best everyday picture is taken from across Vittal Mallya Road. From there the lower part of the building fills the frame and the street runs across the foreground, which gives a sense of scale and a bit of city life.

As an alternative, the open courtyard has a fountain, cafés and marble staircases framed by the building's modern lines. It makes a calmer, closer picture.

Keep your phone level and use the gridlines, because tall buildings look leaning and unsteady if the phone is tilted. Wait for a gap in the traffic or pedestrians if you want a clean foreground. Take a few frames at different heights and keep the best. Inside, shop interiors may restrict photography.
text.geographic_location: UB City is in Bengaluru's central business district, at the corner of Kasturba Road and Vittal Mallya Road. It is opposite Cubbon Park.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the MG Road-Brigade Road junction, which is about 1.8 km away. The mall's address is on Vittal Mallya Road. Once there, cross to the opposite side of Vittal Mallya Road from the mall. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tall building and the street in one frame, then try the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the glass and the arched upper section.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Vittal Mallya Road (opposite side of the road from the mall). The lower part of the building filling the frame, with the street in the foreground. On the opposite side of the road from the mall.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them, so it doesn't lean. Keep the street across the bottom of the frame so the building has something to tower over. If you want a different picture, the courtyard with its fountain and marble staircases is a good second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the glass doesn't turn pale and washed out. Try a Live Photo if people or traffic are moving through the foreground, so you can choose the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight gives the clearest view of the glass and lines. If you come after dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The street view is from a public road, but the mall is a commercial property where shop interiors may restrict photography and professional shoots need permission from mall management, so check the official site before you go.

name: ISKCON Temple Bangalore
label: ISKCON Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ISKCON Temple Bangalore entrance and outer courtyards' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29459362: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'ISKCON Sri Radha Krishna-Chandra Temple' (386 m across).
notes: Large modern Krishna temple complex on a hill.

text.description:
ISKCON Temple Bangalore, on Hare Krishna Hill, is one of the largest Krishna temples in the world. It was inaugurated in May 1997 by India's then president, Shankar Dayal Sharma. The temple is dedicated to Radha Krishna and has six shrines. Two gold-plated features stand out: a flag post 17 m high and a kalash shikhara (the crowning finial) 8.5 m high.

For photographs, the main grand entrance and the outer courtyards are the best places to work from. From there you can fit the front facade and its carved exterior into one frame, with open courtyards and gardens around it. These spaces give you room to step back, which helps with such a large building. Photography is not allowed inside the temple or in the main sanctum, so plan to take all your pictures outdoors. Drones are not permitted on the temple grounds either.

For a second view, walk to the temple pond (the kalyani). The temple rises behind the water, and you can catch its reflection, with the evening fountains in view.

Weekday mornings are described as the quietest time, which makes clear shots of the facade easier. Take a few wide frames of the whole building, then move closer for the carved details and the gold-topped features. Entry arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The temple stands on Hare Krishna Hill, off Chord Road in Rajajinagar, Bangalore.
text.directions_text: No Underground station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the route. Search for ISKCON Temple, Hare Krishna Hill, Chord Road, Rajajinagar. Once you are inside the complex, head for the main grand entrance and the outer courtyards in front of the temple. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and entrance as the eye sees them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyards to fit in the whole front and the open space around it. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carving and the gold-topped features.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The best place to stand is the main grand entrance and outer courtyards, where you can fit in the front facade and carved exterior, framed by the open courtyards and gardens.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the facade centred, with the courtyard space in the foreground to show its scale. Hold the phone level so the vertical lines of the building stay straight. For a different view, try the kalyani (temple pond), where the temple rises behind the water with its reflection and the evening fountains.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the gold parts or bright sky look washed out. Use ultra-wide only when you have space, as it can stretch the edges of the frame. Use night mode for the evening fountains and keep your phone steady against a wall or rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekday mornings are described as the least crowded time. The evening fountains by the pond are worth seeing if you stay later.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship with a temple complex, and photography is not allowed inside, so check the official site before you go for entry arrangements.

name: Vidhana Soudha
label: Vidhana Soudha
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ambedkar Veedhi' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ambedkar Veedhi nearest the subject (our map tiles); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5284317: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Vidhana Soudha' (307 m across).
notes: Grand granite seat of the Karnataka legislature.

text.description:
Vidhana Soudha is the home of Karnataka's two legislative houses, and it is one of the most imposing buildings in Bangalore. It was finished in 1956 in the Neo-Dravidian style. Its pink and black granite gives it a solid, warm look, and the design borrows from temple architecture and from the Mysore Palace. The front faces east. It has a row of 12 tall granite columns and a broad flight of 45 steps leading up to the porch. Above it all sits a central dome about 18 metres across, topped with the State Emblem of India. The whole complex covers around 60 acres, and it is described as the largest state legislature and secretariat building in India. It was meant to be a 'people's palace', and the front shows that ambition clearly.

It photographs well because the symmetry is so strong. A straight-on shot from the road opposite shows the full granite front, the columns, the steps and the dome in one frame. Keep your phone level, switch on the gridlines and line the dome up with the middle of the picture. Because the building is so wide, you will want to step back or use the ultra-wide lens to fit it all in. Be polite around the security staff, and keep your phone pointed at the building rather than at people.
text.geographic_location: Vidhana Soudha stands in Bangalore, with Cubbon Park nearby. The High Court is nearby, and the main front looks onto Ambedkar Veedhi.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head to Ambedkar Veedhi, the road facing the front of the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole front, including the steps and the sky above the dome. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome, the row of columns or the emblem on top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ambedkar Veedhi (opposite the front facade, on the road side). The full granite front of the building with its central dome and grand approach, framed straight on from across the road. From here you see the full granite front with its central dome and grand approach, straight on from across the road. Stay on the pavement and keep clear of the traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome on the central vertical line so both sides of the front match. Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the granite. If you want a quieter, softer view, walk to Cubbon Park and shoot the building across the shaded lawns. For the lit-up look at dusk, try Cubbon Park Road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use night mode for the evening shots, and rest your elbows against your body or a wall so the picture stays sharp. Take a few frames in case people or cars wander into the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 7–8 AM, is quiet for traffic. The building is lit mainly on Sunday and public-holiday evenings, so a weekday evening visit may find it unlit. The best hour varies, so check on the day and choose between a calm morning and a lit evening.

text.access_note: The exterior can generally be photographed from the road, but this is a working government building with security and restricted areas, so check the official site before you go and follow any staff instructions.

photo.artist: Muhammad Mahdi Karim www.micro2macro.net and Mydreamsparrow

name: Attara Kacheri
label: Attara Kacheri
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dr. Ambedkar Veedhi' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Dr. B. R. Ambedkar Station, Vidhana Soudha' (node/6400857556): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/446900: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Karnataka High Court' (352 m across).
notes: Red Neo-Dravidian building opposite Vidhana Soudha.

text.description: Attara Kacheri is the red-painted home of the Karnataka High Court in central Bangalore. It is a two-storey neoclassical building of stone and brick, built between 1864 and 1868, with a symmetrical front and classical columns. Its strong red stands out against the greenery of Cubbon Park behind it. Across the road is the white granite Vidhana Soudha, and the contrast between the two buildings is what makes the picture. The building almost came down: in 1982 there was a proposal to demolish it. The first public interest litigation ever filed in the court was brought to stop that, and the plan was dropped in 1985. It was later renovated and extended with new blocks in the same style. For your photo, stand on the Vidhana Soudha side of the road and shoot the red front with the trees of Cubbon Park behind it. The stretch is close to Vidhana Soudha Metro station. Remember that this is a working court. You can photograph only the outside, and it is best to be discreet near the court entrances. Check that the frontage is clear before you go, as construction has blocked the view on at least one visit.
text.geographic_location: In central Bangalore, on Dr. Ambedkar Veedhi, on the edge of Cubbon Park. It stands directly opposite the Vidhana Soudha, the seat of the Karnataka Legislature.
text.directions_text: The nearest Metro stop is Vidhana Soudha station, and the viewing spot on Dr. Ambedkar Veedhi is close to it. Security checks at the station can be strict, so allow a little extra time. Once you are in the Vidhana Soudha area, cross to the Vidhana Soudha side of the road and look towards the red building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole red façade with the trees behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the building in. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the columns and the symmetrical centre of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Dr. Ambedkar Veedhi (opposite the building, on the Vidhana Soudha side of the road, facing the red façade). The red neo-classical front of Attara Kacheri, framed by the white granite of Vidhana Soudha across the road and the greenery of Cubbon Park behind. Stand on Dr. From here you face the red front of Attara Kacheri, which lies to the south-east. The two buildings face each other across the road, and the greenery of Cubbon Park is behind the court.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the centre of the building up with the middle of the frame so the symmetry looks tidy. Keep the phone level to stop the columns leaning. For a quieter, wider picture of the red façade against trees and lawns, Cubbon Park is a good alternative viewpoint. You can also take a straight-on or close view of the front, but only from outside.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red wall to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the red stays rich and any bright sky or white stonework is not washed out. Do not use portrait mode, because it does not suit a building. If cars pass in front, take a few shots and keep the clearest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning and late afternoon are described as pleasant times to visit, and they are good for photos too.

text.access_note: This is an active High Court, so only the exterior can be photographed and there is no interior access.
claims_not_in_sources: Gentler morning and late-afternoon light tends to suit the red colour of the building.
Slightly lowering the exposure helps keep red and white surfaces from washing out in bright light.
Passing traffic on the road may get in the way of the view.

name: Commercial Street
label: Commercial Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Commercial Street' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q24943501: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description: Commercial Street is one of the oldest and busiest shopping streets in Bangalore, and that is exactly what makes it good for phone photos. It is a lively, close-packed street of clothes, footwear, jewellery and electronics shops, with food places mixed in. The shopping spreads into the side lanes too, including Dispensary Road and Abrahim Sahab Street. The street runs between OPH Road and K Kamraj Road in Tasker Town, in the middle of the Central Business District. The pictures here come from colour and movement: painted shopfronts, bright shutters, shoppers and street vendors all in one view. Walk along the pavement and shoot down the line of shopfronts, so the street leads the eye into the frame. The older houses and by-lanes can make a calmer backdrop when the main street is packed. It is one of the most crowded streets in the city, with very little parking, so expect people in every shot and keep your phone close when you stop to frame a picture. A weekday morning is the easiest time for a clear view. If you want a quieter, older-feeling subject nearby, Russell Market in Shivajinagar is a good alternative, though it does not show Commercial Street itself.

text.description: The Bull Temple (Dodda Basavana Gudi) is a Basavanagudi landmark, famous for its huge granite Nandi bull. The temple sits on a rocky outcrop, and that setting is part of what makes it photograph well. Guides recommend a wider view from the neighbouring Bugle Rock Park, where an old watchtower stands on a raised rock. From there you can look back over the temple and the Basavanagudi rooftops, with trees framing the scene. Guides recommend the park for photography beyond the temple itself, and the rock with its watchtower is named as the park's main attraction. For a close shot, the outer courtyard of the temple lets you fill the frame with the Nandi, with the carved walls and roof around it. Photography is allowed in the outer courtyard and the park, but not in the inner sanctum, so ask temple staff if you are unsure. A Ganesha temple nearby also does not permit photography inside. Drones are generally not permitted at the site. Plan on two photos: a wide scene from the rock, then a tighter portrait of the bull from the courtyard. Dress respectfully, as this is a working place of worship.
text.geographic_location: In Basavanagudi, in the south of Bangalore, along Bull Temple Road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Basavanagudi and ask for Bugle Rock Park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the rock to take in the trees, the watchtower and the town beyond. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the temple and rooftops in the distance, or the carved details in the courtyard.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Bugle Rock Park (the rock outcrop with the watchtower, looking back over the temple and Basavanagudi). A wider view of the temple complex and its surroundings from the slightly raised rock, with the trees and the old watchtower in the scene. Check the map for the exact position of the rock and watchtower in Bugle Rock Park, and aim for the rock outcrop by the watchtower. Look north and the temple will be a distant element among the trees and Basavanagudi rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line. Use a tree branch or the watchtower as a foreground frame to add depth. For a second picture, Dodda Basavana Gudi's outer courtyard lets you fill the frame with the granite Nandi, with the temple roof and carved walls around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the temple to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and keep it out of the inner sanctum.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, going by general guide advice for the area.

text.access_note: The temple is a place of worship with no photography in the inner sanctum, so dress respectfully and ask temple staff before you go.

text.description:
Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace is a two-storey teak building in the old part of Bangalore. The front is all arches, slim wooden pillars and upper-floor balconies, and from the garden you can see the whole facade at once. The lawn in front gives you a clean, uncluttered foreground, so the building stands out well against the sky.

Hyder Ali began the palace in 1781, inside the walls of Bangalore Fort, and it was finished in 1791 in Tipu Sultan's time. It was Tipu's summer residence, and it is believed he held his court from the balconies on the upper floor. The ground floor is now a small museum. The Archaeological Survey of India looks after the palace, and the garden and lawn at the front are kept up by the state horticulture department.

For a phone photo, start on the front lawn and face the facade. Turn on gridlines to keep the building level in the frame. Then step in closer for a second shot of the carved wood pillars and balconies. If the front gate is the only place you can reach, the palace also looks good seen set back across the garden through the gate from Albert Victor Road. The palace sits inside a ticketed compound, and photography rules seem to vary, so check the entry rules with the Archaeological Survey of India before you go.
text.geographic_location: The palace is in the middle of Old Bangalore, in the area near the Kalasipalya bus stand, on the site of the old Bangalore Fort. Albert Victor Road is a place to see the palace through the gate.
text.directions_text: Start from the Kalasipalya bus stand in Old Bangalore, as the palace is near it. The phone icon on the map is at the palace grounds, on the front garden and lawn. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the building and cannot fit it all in. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details of the pillars and balconies.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The teak arches, pillars and balconies make up the view, with the lawn as your foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the building level. Leave a band of lawn at the bottom as a clean foreground. For a second shot, zoom in on the wooden pillars and balconies. As an alternative, from Albert Victor Road you can photograph the palace set back across the garden, seen through the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the wood keeps its colour. Keep the phone upright so the vertical pillars do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the light is soft and the sun is not directly behind the building.

text.access_note: The palace and its lawn sit inside a ticketed compound run by the Archaeological Survey of India, and photography rules vary, so check the entry rules with the Archaeological Survey of India before you go.

name: Ulsoor Lake
label: Ulsoor Lake
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ulsoor Lake' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ulsoor Lake' (relation/1857615): edge nearest the subject (1341 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1857615: large area 'Ulsoor Lake' (1346 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Popular lake with boating and skyline views.

text.description:
Ulsoor Lake, also called Halasuru Lake, is one of the biggest lakes in Bangalore. It covers about 50 hectares and has several small islands. The lake goes back to Kempe Gowda's time, but the shape you see today was created by Lewin Bentham Bowring, a Commissioner of Bangalore. For a phone photographer, the appeal is the calm water. Lakeside trees and the city skyline can both appear as reflections, which gives a simple, layered picture without much effort.

Separately, local travel guides single out the eastern bank as the area for reflections with the city behind. Sunrise and sunset are the best moments, when the light is soft and the surface is usually at its stillest. Start with a wide shot that includes the trees, the water and a slice of skyline. Then try a closer frame of a single tree and its reflection.

A second viewpoint is worth a look if you have time: Kensington Road, on the lake's western edge, is recommended for sunset light across the water. Part of the lake is controlled by the Madras Engineer Group and the rest by the city corporation, so not every shoreline is open to walkers. Some of the surroundings were reported to be under renovation, so conditions may vary on the day.
text.geographic_location: Ulsoor Lake is on the eastern side of Bangalore, in the Halasuru area close to M G Road.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the M G Road area, close to Halasuru, and go by taxi or hired scooter to the lake. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of water, trees and skyline. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and a bigger sweep of the bank. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out an island or a single tree.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Ulsoor Lake (eastern bank of the lake). Reflections of the lakeside trees and the Bangalore skyline in the water, best framed at sunrise or sunset. Local guides recommend the eastern bank as the area for skyline reflections, so if access allows, that is where the lakeside trees and the Bangalore skyline are most likely to appear reflected in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower third line so the reflection fills the lower half of the frame. Keep your phone level so the horizon stays straight. Hold it low and close to the water for a stronger reflection. For a different view, try the western edge on Kensington Road at sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky colours are not washed out. Wait for a calm moment between ripples. Panorama mode works well if you hold the phone steady and sweep slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and sunset, when the light is low and the reflections are at their best.

text.access_note: Parts of the lake are managed by the Madras Engineer Group and the city corporation, so access to the shoreline can vary; check the official site or local signs for access details and conditions before you go.

text.description: The Museum of Art & Photography, usually shortened to MAP, is a private museum on Kasturba Road in Bangalore. It holds more than 20,000 works, mostly from the Indian subcontinent, covering art, textiles, photography, craft and design from the twelfth century to today. The museum opened its doors to the public on 18 February 2023, after starting life online in 2020. The building has five floors and about 44,000 square feet of space. It was designed by Mathew & Ghosh Architects and includes galleries, an auditorium, a library and a sculpture garden. For a phone photographer, the main subject is the building itself: a large, modern shape that suits a straight-on view, an angled corner shot, or a close-up of its materials and lines. Start with one wide picture that shows the whole front and its surroundings, then move in for details such as textures, shadows and entrances. If you plan to photograph inside, rules on photography in the galleries can differ from room to room, so check the official site before you go. Stay out of doorways and walkways while you shoot.

text.description:
The Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum sits in Cubbon Park and is a science and technology museum that draws nearly one million visitors a year. It was opened in 1962 by Jawaharlal Nehru and named in memory of Sir M. Visvesvaraya. The original building covered about 4,000 square metres. An extension in 1979 raised that to roughly 6,900 square metres, so it is a large building to fit into one phone frame. Inside, the galleries cover engines, electricity, space technology, biotechnology and electronics. There is also a science area for children.

The museum photographs well because the exterior and the exhibits are both good subjects. Outside, the building is set among the park's greenery, which gives a pleasant contrast with the architecture. Inside, you can find big mechanical shapes such as the jet aircraft engine in the Engine Hall, a full-size model of the Wright Brothers' Flyer, and a moving Spinosaurus replica in the Dinosaur Alive exhibit. The Science for Kids gallery has a mirror maze, which is a fun place for a reflection shot.

For the exterior, step well back so the whole front fits, and keep the phone level using the gridlines. For close details, move in on one exhibit at a time rather than trying to capture a whole hall. Indoor photography rules can vary by gallery, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is inside Cubbon Park in Bangalore. It is set among the park's trees.
text.directions_text: No Metro station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Cubbon Park in Bangalore and look for the museum building inside the park. The building is large, about 160 metres across, so it is easy to spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the building from outside and for big halls inside. Use the default lens (1x) for most exhibit shots. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as engine parts or signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a full-building photo, walk back from the building to the edge of the grounds, then turn and face it. Inside, stand at the entrance of a gallery to get depth in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the walls straight. Try to include some of the park's trees at the edges to give the building context. Inside, frame a single large exhibit, such as the jet engine or the Wright Flyer model, against the open space behind it. In the mirror maze, hold the phone at chest height and keep your own reflection small in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the screen to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly to keep the sky and building facade from washing out. Indoors, hold the phone steady with both hands, and use night mode if the gallery is dim and the shot looks grainy.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning for softer light on the exterior and fewer people in the galleries. Weekends and school holidays are likely to be busier. Check the official site before you go for current visiting times.

label: Bangalore Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bangalore Fort' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/38751029: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bangalore Fort' (150 m across).
notes: Remains of Kempegowda and Tipu's fort.

text.description:
Bangalore Fort is what is left of the walled stronghold that gave the old city its start. Kempe Gowda I began it in 1537 as a mud fort. Hyder Ali rebuilt it in stone in 1761, and his son Tipu Sultan strengthened it later in the 18th century. British East India Company troops under Lord Cornwallis took it on 21 March 1791, breaching the wall near the Delhi Gate. Today the Delhi Gate and two bastions are the main parts still standing, and a marble plaque marks the spot where the wall was broken. The fort once ran to about a mile around, so what you see now is only a small piece of it.

For a phone photo, the best idea is to turn your back on the gate and walk onto the inside lawn and garden, then shoot back toward it. The tended grass and planting in the foreground give the weathered stone something soft to sit against, and that is what makes the picture work. Keep the frame simple: gate or bastion in the upper half, lawn filling the lower half. If you want the carved granite gateway straight-on from the front, Delhi Gate is a good second picture. Check the current Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) rules before you go, as they may limit what equipment you can bring and use.
text.geographic_location: Bangalore Fort stands at New Tharagupet in the old part of the city, close to KR Market. The Delhi Gate faces Krishnarajendra Road.
text.directions_text: Start from KR Market, the well-known area next to the fort. By taxi or hired scooter, ask for Bangalore Fort or Delhi Gate at New Tharagupet. Once there, walk through to the grounds and head for the lawn and garden inside, where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a clean view of the gate or bastion with the lawn in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more grass and sky, or if the gate will not fit from where you are standing. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the stonework and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The gate or bastion is in view, with the green lawn and garden in the foreground as a backdrop. The tended garden is what visitors usually mention as the good setting here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the gate or bastion on one of the upper lines, with the lawn filling the lower third or half. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. As a different shot, Delhi Gate seen straight-on from the front shows the carved stone gateway with its granite walls and bastion.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. Take a few frames at 0.5x and 1x and compare them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and fewer harsh shadows on the lawn. Avoid the middle of a sunny day if you can.

text.access_note: Check the current Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) rules before you go, especially for tripods, drones or other equipment beyond your phone.

text.description: St. Mark's Cathedral is a Church of South India cathedral at the west end of Mahatma Gandhi Road in MacIver Town. It began as a garrison church for the East India Company's Madras Army. The foundation stone was laid in 1808, building finished in 1812, and it was consecrated in 1816. It was later enlarged and rebuilt after a fire in 1923 and a collapse in 1924, and the version you see today was completed in 1927. The style is English Baroque, inspired by St Paul's Cathedral in London, with a dome, round Roman arches and a tower. That mix of classical columns and a colonial look is why it photographs so well from the street. From the Mahatma Gandhi Road side you can fit the portico, the columns and the tower into one frame, with the tree-lined compound around them. Guides often treat this as the most recognisable view of the church. If you want something softer and quieter, Sri Chamarajendra Park is a recommended alternative viewpoint, with the cathedral seen through the park trees. Keep your phone upright for the tower and portico, or turn it sideways to include the trees and the width of the front. Photography inside may be restricted, so be discreet and ask staff if you are unsure. The main Sunday service is at 10:30 AM, so avoid shooting around then.
text.geographic_location: St. Mark's Cathedral is in MacIver Town, central Bangalore, at the west end of Mahatma Gandhi Road.
text.directions_text: There are no Metro or train stops listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the west end of Mahatma Gandhi Road in MacIver Town. Check the best frontage position on Mahatma Gandhi Road on the day and adjust until the whole front fits.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the tower on a vertical line so the building does not lean. Use the trees on either side as a natural frame. For a calmer alternative, try Sri Chamarajendra Park, where the cathedral appears through the park trees, and check the exact position on the ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the detail. If a lot of traffic passes, take a few photos in a row and pick the clearest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go outside service times and avoid the main Sunday service at 10:30 AM. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the front.

text.description: Venkatappa Art Gallery is a modernist building in the vicinity of Cubbon Park, next to the Bangalore Museum and the Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum. It shows the paintings, sculpture and other work of K. Venkatappa (1886-1965), one of Karnataka's best-known artists. It also holds collections of KK Hebbar and the sculptor Rajaram. The foundation stone was laid on 24 November 1967 and the building was finished in 1975. It was designed to look like an artificial island, with a moat and lotus pond around it, so the modernist lines of the building are set against water and greenery. Only three of the five planned floors were built, which gives it a low, solid shape. That makes it easy to photograph as a clean architectural subject. Move a few steps to find a clear view of the whole building, then move in for smaller shots of the modernist lines, the water around the base and the reflections. Look for people crossing the approach, which adds scale. The gallery is often mistaken for its neighbour the Bangalore Museum, so check the name on the building before you start shooting.

text.description: St Mary's Basilica is a Gothic-style church in Shivajinagar, the area once known as Blackpally. It photographs well because the tall tower and spires rise above the busy streets around it. The best phone shot here is not a straight-on picture of the front. It is the approach: walk towards the church along Commercial Street and the tower appears at the far end of the street, with market life in the foreground. That gives you a layered street scene with the church as the destination. The church was rebuilt between 1856 and 1882 and consecrated on 8 September 1882. In 1973 it became a minor basilica, the first church in Karnataka to hold that status. The arches, ornamental details and stained glass are Gothic in style, and the columns and spires can be seen from a long way off. Every September a ten-day feast fills the surrounding streets, ending with a chariot procession. It is lively to see, but processions can block your view of the church. Outside the feast, Sundays and feast days are the busiest times, so a weekday visit gives you more room to frame the tower. If you want the full front of the church, Msgr. F. Noronha Road shows the Gothic facade with its tower and spire against the streets of Shivajinagar. Russel Market Square gives a quieter, wider view across the open space.
text.geographic_location: St Mary's Basilica stands in the Shivajinagar (Blackpally) area of Bangalore. Commercial Street and Russel Market are close by.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or stop is listed for this spot; head for Shivajinagar and navigate to St Mary's Basilica. Walk towards the tower and keep it in view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street scene, so the tower sits small at the end of the street with the market around it. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the tower closer and squeeze the street together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only once you reach the church and want the whole front and spire in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Commercial Street (walking towards the church from the Commercial Street end). The tower appearing at the far end of the busy street, with market life in the foreground. Face north-west and walk towards the church from the Commercial Street end. From here the tower appears at the far end of the busy street, with market life in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines, so the street leads the eye to it. Keep some stalls or people in the foreground for depth. If you want a clean shot of the full front, Msgr. F. Noronha Road or Russel Market Square are good alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays pale blue instead of white. Take a few frames, because people keep moving through the scene. Live Photos or motion can capture the movement of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a weekday, early in the day if you can, when the street is quieter. Avoid Sundays, feast days and the September feast if you want a clear view of the tower.

text.access_note: The basilica is an active place of worship and the streets around it are public; interior photography may be restricted during services and flash is discouraged, so check the official site before you go.

notes: One of India's oldest museums, near Cubbon Park.

text.description: The Government Museum is a neoclassical building on Kasturba Road, next to the Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum and the Venkatappa Art Gallery. It was built in 1877 and is one of the oldest museums in India. The museum was founded in 1865, first sat in the old Cantonment jail building, and moved into this purpose-built home in 1877. The design has two porticos, Corinthian columns, circular arches, sloping eaves and a strong parapet wall. These repeating columns and arches give the front a clear, symmetrical look that suits a phone camera well. Inside, the collection includes sculpture, coins, old jewellery and inscriptions, among them the Halmidi inscription, the earliest known Kannada inscription (450 AD). For photos, the best subject is the façade itself. Fit the portico and the columns in one shot, using the ultra-wide lens if you cannot step back, and turn on gridlines so the vertical lines stay straight. If you have room, step to one side to catch the building at a slight angle, which shows the depth of the columns. Its neighbours make it easy to combine several stops in one visit. Reports say the museum has been closed for renovation, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In central Bangalore on Kasturba Road, close to the Cantonment area. It stands between the Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum and the Venkatappa Art Gallery.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Kasturba Road area in central Bangalore and head for the Government Museum on Kasturba Road. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is at the museum itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front of the building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the portico and cannot step back, and keep the phone level to limit leaning walls. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the column tops and arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the façade and keep the portico in the centre of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines. Centre the portico for a balanced, symmetrical shot, or step a little to one side for a slight angle that shows the depth of the columns. Include some of the ground in front for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky does not wash out the building's detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the façade is less harsh than at midday.

text.access_note: Access and opening may change, as the museum is a government-run site that has been reported closed for renovation, so check the official site before you go.
